title: Biosensor Cell-Fit-HD4D for correlation of single-cell fate and microscale energy deposition in complex ion beams
protocol: Remove the glass bottom of a 6-well plate by applying physical force with a forceps.
Thoroughly clean the adhesive surface from residual glue using 70% EtOH and low-lint laboratory tissues.
Ensure complete removal of residual glass.
Mix small drops of tissue glue around the adhesive surface edge of the well using a micropipette.
Use approximately 8 drops totaling about 1 μL per well.
Place the well plate upside down and attach the dry FNTD wafer to the well bottom using forceps or a suction contact lens holder.
Incubate the plate upside-down at 37°C in a cell culture incubator for approximately 3 min for the tissue glue to polymerize.
Sterilize the modified wells with 70% EtOH (ethanol).
Wash the wells once with PBS.
Aspirate any excess fluid and check for potential leakages on tissue paper.
Fill the modified wells with cell culture medium or PBS.
Place the plate on several tissue sheets in an incubator at 37°C for a recommended minimum of 6 h–12 h to guarantee complete, durable sealing.
Aspirate the medium.
Gently wipe the back side of the FNTD wafer with 70% EtOH.
Retrace the marks of the optical axis of the FNTD wafer for later readout.
Wash cells according to standard cell culture procedure.
Trypsinize cells according to standard cell culture procedure.
Collect and count cells according to standard cell culture procedure.
Seed suitable cell numbers in standard medium in the modified wells.
Incubate the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate at room temperature for approximately 20 min to obtain homogenous cell distribution within the well.
Incubate under cell culture conditions (37°C, 5% CO2) for a minimum of 4 h for cell attachment.
Set up an imaging protocol with appropriate parameters.
Start imaging immediately following irradiation.
Record a z-stack covering approximately 100 μm in axial dimension and the overlying cell layer.
Compile at least two imaging programs for the same positions.
Perform long-term imaging of the cell layer only.
Set up initial readout imaging program.
Define positions to be scanned based on a 6-well plate dummy or the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate.
Scan FNTD and tumor cells in a single step for the initial stack.
Record earliest cellular response irradiation and spinels as landmarks.
Capture an image stack of approximately 30 imaging planes for the initial stack.
Perform live-cell imaging with an image stack of approximately 3 imaging planes using widefield microscopy.
Transfer Cell-Fit-HD4D to confocal microscopy to read out FNTD.
Reconstruct each ion track into the cell layer recorded in the initial readout using image registration routines.
Set the z-stack range with intervals of ≤ 3 μm.
Determine the z-range for the initial stack using autofocus or manual offset based on the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate.
Select light channels for visualization of the cell layer.
Determine proper exposure time(s) for the selected light channels.
Select transmitted light channel to visualize spinels within the FNTD crystal structure.
Keep transmitted light exposure to a minimum due to phototoxicity risks for long-term imaging.
Set the exposure time for the cell imaging channel lower compared to time-lapse imaging.
Set autofocus, image save location, and other parameters according to discretion.
Save the program settings.
Set up time-lapse imaging program.
Ensure exact same imaging positions are taken over from the initial stack.
Select light channels and determine proper exposure time(s) for time-lapse imaging.
Select scanning intervals.
Set scanning intervals between 15-45 minutes based on experimental requirements.
Balance phototoxicity and cell traceability when choosing scanning intervals.
Set autofocus parameters according to discretion.
Define z-stacks parameters as needed.
Specify image save location.
Save imaging program settings.
Load imaging programs into a queue for immediate acquisition.
Prepare Cell-Fit-HD4D for 5 minutes.
Setup irradiation equipment for 20 minutes.
Conduct ion irradiation for 2 minutes.
Irradiate the cell layer with a horizontal carbon ion beam.
Position the cell layer in the middle of a 1 cm wide spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) at a water equivalent depth of ∼3.5 cm.
Apply physical dose levels of 1 Gy and 0.5 Gy, resulting in expected carbon ion beam fluences of 8.43 ∗ 10^6 cm^-2 and 4.16 ∗ 10^6 cm^-2, respectively.
Align the biosensor perpendicular to the incoming ion beam.
Place additional stopping material in front of the well plate to position cells at the desired Bragg peak location.
Heat the microscope 2–4 hours before irradiation to prevent thermal expansion errors during imaging.
Set up and save the imaging program prior to irradiation to minimize delay between irradiation and imaging.
Position and place potential stopping material (e.g., PMMA) according to planned physical dose level to achieve desired linear energy transfer (LET) and ion beam fluence in FNTD and cell layer.
Shield control well positions with additional stopping material as required.
Seal the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate in a laminar hood.
Switch to phenol-free medium at this point for improved signal-noise ratio in red channel.
Remove the lid of the plate and cover wells with a single piece of flexible wax-polyolefin film.
Apply gentle pressure on well edges after covering.
Place a tissue with the approximate size of the plate on top of the wax sealing to maintain pressure during irradiation.
Close the plate lid and seal the plate by wrapping the sides in flexible wax-polyolefin film while applying firm pressure to the lid.
Incubate the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate at cell culture conditions until irradiation.
Position the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate perpendicular to the ion beam path, with the FNTD wafers in direct contact with the phantoms.
Confirm sealing of the plate.
Start irradiation program.
Transfer the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate to the widefield microscope as quickly as possible.
Remove the sealing from the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate.
Place the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate on the microscope stage.
Apply the lid of a potentially associated micro incubator.
Start program.
Aspirate medium from the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate.
Wash 1× with PBS.
Fix cells using the chosen method, such as EtOH-fixation at -20°C overnight.
Wash 1× with PBS.
Apply blocking/permeabilization buffer (1% Triton-X-100, 3% BSA in PBS) for 20 min at room temperature.
Cover the FNTD wafer with primary antibody diluted in washing buffer (blocking buffer 1:5 diluted in PBS), approximately 100 μL/well.
Incubate overnight at 4°C.
Alternatively, incubate at room temperature for 3–4 h.
Wash 2× in washing buffer, 5 min each.
Cover the FNTD wafer with secondary antibody diluted in washing buffer (blocking buffer 1:5 diluted in PBS), approximately 100 μL/well.
Incubate 4–6 h at 4°C.
Alternatively, incubate at room temperature for 1 h.
Wash 1× in washing buffer for 5 minutes.
Add DAPI or alternative nuclear dyes such as DRAQ5 if desired.
Wash 1× in PBS for 5 minutes.
Store in PBS at 4°C until imaging.
Reload previously imaged positions from the saved setup used for time-lapse microscopy.
Yield staining signals after FNTD scan on the laser scanning microscope.
Acquire microscopy images of ion trajectories in the FNTD in the form of track spots.
Concurrently acquire spinels to enable precise image registration with previous widefield imaging.
Place the Cell-Fit-HD4D plate including PBS in case of cells to be imaged on the CLSM stage.
Locate the areas imaged during the initial readout.
Scan the imaged area of the FNTD using a 40× oil objective.
Ensure that the entire imaging area acquired in the initial readout is covered.
Set sufficient field of view (∼220 × 220 μm²) and limit the number of tiles needed for the entire imaging area (∼660 × 660 μm²).
Make sure that single imaging tiles have ∼20 μm overlap for subsequent stitching to gain complete imaging field.
Adjust laser power, dwell time, and number of re-scans in CLSM accordingly for sufficient signal-to-noise ratio.
Place stained cells on a widefield microscope for imaging.
Scan the cell layer if additional biomolecules have been stained.
Ensure identical positions are used for correlation of recorded signals and physical energy deposition.
Avoid excitation wavelength close to 405 nm prior to FNTD readout to prevent bleaching.
Combine the data sets of the cell layer acquired in the initial readout and subsequent live-cell imaging.
Perform maximum intensity z projections of the acquired image stack for each time point.

Segment and track cells/ cell nuclei using LevelSet Tracker or other tracking algorithms which register mitotic events to gain time series of the black white (BW) masks of the cross-sectional areas of the tracked objects.
Export single frame images to a distinct folder designated for each single cell.
Manually control cell masks for precise nuclei segmentation.
Adjust tracking algorithm parameters as necessary for correct ion track-cell-assignment.
Apply an algorithm to recognize topological changes in mitotic cells for progeny tracking.
Complement the automatic tracking with user-guided control and correction for high cell densities.
Track cells based on the pan-nuclear signal of the 53BP1-mCherry fusion protein.
Analyze RIF for single cells over time.
Quantify RIF number, size, and signal intensity.
Use trainable WEKA segmentation in ImageJ for RIF analysis.
Adjust tracking algorithms and parameters according to cell signals.
Segment and measure extra-nuclear readout signals using transmitted light channel if necessary.
Apply the cell mask of the last scanned time-lapse frame on the post-time-lapse staining channel.
Measure the respective signal.
Quantify nuclear p21 signal.
Correlate quantified p21 signal with initially deposited energies to determine potential energy-dependent growth arrest.
Use recorded track spots for ion track reconstruction in the FNTD and extrapolation into the cell layer.
Assign extrapolated ion tracks to cell nuclei.
Compute the energy deposition in individual cell nucleus using the intensity of the track spots.
Perform stitching of the recorded FNTD data sets according to Niklas et al., 2016, to gain a single data set simplifying subsequent ion track reconstruction.
Test for optical aberrations of the applied objectives and limit them if necessary.
Record an imaging field of approximately 660 × 660 μm² using widefield microscopy with a 20× objective.
Capture 4 × 4 confocal tiles using a 40× objective to ensure complete coverage of the initial readout area.
Ensure an overlap of approximately 20 μm between single tiles for high accuracy in stitching.
Use the FNTD package as a plugin for ImageJ/Fiji software to identify and link track spots.
Perform linear regression analysis to fit the ion trajectory into a line based on linked track spots.
Extrapolate the ion trajectories into the cell layer using the slopes of the trajectory in both xz and yz directions.
Apply maximum intensity z projections to reduce the dimensionality of the cell layer from 3D to 2D.
Extrapolate the ion tracks into the center of the cell layer in the vertical position, for example at 2 μm.
Apply image registration to datasets from widefield and confocal microscopy.
Calculate the intersection of extrapolated ion trajectories with BW masks of cell nuclei using a logical AND operation.
Compute LET and deposited dose in the cell nucleus or object of interest based on track spot intensity.
Match detected track spots' intensity distribution with Monte Carlo generated LET distribution for irradiation setup.
Count the number of ion hits intersecting the BW mask of each cell nucleus/object to determine beam fluence.
Fuse the data on energy deposition and molecular dynamics/ gene expression/ cellular fate.
Correlate biological readouts to physical beam parameters.
